description: Somos un equipo formado por estudiantes de la Facultad de Ingeniería Mecánica y Eléctrica en la UANL
summary: We developed NASA Analog Finder, a large-scale geospatial web platform and satellite data pipeline that identifies and ranks Earth locations serving as high-fidelity scientific analogs for Moon and Mars exploration.Our solution addresses the challenge by benchmarking 42 lunar and Martian expedition zones—extracted from NASA Mars/Moon Trek (including Jezero, Gale, and Shackleton craters)—against a massive dataset of 2,029 analyzed terrestrial sites. Using a Python and pandas backend connected to Microsoft Planetary Computer and NASA Giovanni, we automated the extraction of real satellite observations from NASADEM, MODIS, and Landsat to compute terrain slope, surface temperature extremes, thermal amplitude Delta T, vegetation index (NDVI), aerosol optical depth, and sulfate ratios. The Leaflet.js frontend runs a real-time similarity engine across all 2,029 Earth candidates and features a custom parameter builder ("Add It Yourself"), accelerating field-testing validation and reducing technical risks for future Artemis and Mars missions.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

NASA Analog Finder is a global-scale geospatial decision-support platform that quantitatively evaluates, compares, and ranks 2,029 Earth locations against 42 lunar and Martian landing and expedition zones, identifying which terrestrial environments best replicate their physical, thermal, and topographic conditions.

Its architecture operates in two stages to combine massive scientific processing with instant user interactivity:

  • Large-Scale Satellite Data Pipeline (Offline Backend): An automated Python engine processed coordinates for 2,029 terrestrial sites (volcanic fields, lava tubes, hyper-arid deserts, impact craters, and polar dry valleys). Through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, it queried three official satellite collections per site:
    1. NASADEM: Extracted Digital Elevation Models (DEM) to mathematically compute average terrain Slope (°).
    2. MODIS (modis-11A1-061): Retrieved day/night land surface temperatures to determine Temp_Max (°C), Temp_Min (°C), and Thermal Amplitude ($\Delta T$).
    3. Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 (landsat-c2-l2): Processed spectral bands to compute Vegetation Index (NDVI) and shortwave infrared ratios (swir16 / swir22) as a mineralogical proxy for Sulfur/Sulfates.
    4. NASA Giovanni & Mars/Moon Trek: Integrated Aerosol Optical Depth (Dust) metrics and benchmarked them against 42 lunar and Martian expedition zones profiled via NASA Mars Trek and NASA Moon Trek (TES and LRO Diviner datasets).
  • Interactive Similarity Engine (Real-Time Frontend): The web interface consumes the pre-processed JSON matrix of 2,029 terrestrial sites and runs a client-side multivariate similarity algorithm against any of the 42 space targets, rendering dynamic map markers, side-by-side comparison tables, and official NASA/USGS references in real time.

2. How is our project creative?

  • Massive Cross-Planetary Scale & The "Add It Yourself" Custom Mission Builder: Instead of limiting users to a handful of well-known deserts, we built a planetary search engine capable of cross-referencing 42 off-world expedition profiles against 2,029 Earth sites (over 85,000 possible site-to-target comparisons). Furthermore, we engineered an interactive "Add It Yourself" ("Agrégalo tú") mode where mission planners can input custom environmental constraints. If any input is left blank, our JavaScript engine dynamically recalculates parameter weights, excluding empty fields without breaking the mathematical model.
  • Zero-Latency Hybrid Architecture: Querying satellite rasters for 2,029 sites live would take hours. By decoupling heavy raster mining in the backend (Python/pandas) from client-side visualization (lightweight JSON + Leaflet.js), users and judges can filter and recalculate all 2,029 global locations in milliseconds with zero server lag or API rate-limit failures.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

  • De-risking Space Exploration: With 42 lunar and Martian expedition zones modeled (spanning historic landing sites, active rover zones, and future Artemis candidate regions), space agencies and robotics teams can instantly pinpoint which of the 2,029 Earth locations serves as the highest-fidelity proving ground for rovers, EVA suits, habitats, and ISRU drills.
  • Democratizing Field Research: By scanning over two thousand terrestrial locations, our algorithm surfaces overlooked, high-accuracy analog sites across Latin America (such as El Pinacate in Mexico and Atacama/Chajnantor in Chile) and developing regions worldwide, empowering university teams to conduct validated field tests closer to home.

4. Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Languages & Environment: Python 3.10+, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, developed using VS Code, Google Cloud Shell (Code OSS), and Git/GitHub.
  • Data Science & Geospatial Stack: pandas and numpy for cleaning and structuring the 2,029 Earth records and 42 planetary targets; pystac-client, planetary-computer, and raster processing libraries.
  • Frontend & Mapping: Leaflet.js (high-performance rendering of thousands of interactive markers without paid API key barriers) and Vite.
  • NASA Data & Portals: NASA Mars Trek, NASA Moon Trek, NASA Giovanni, NASA Worldview, NASADEM, MODIS, and NASA/USGS Landsat.
  • AI & Coding Assistants: Generative AI tools and coding agents (OpenCode / Gemini) for batch pipeline automation, STAC query optimization, and technical documentation.

5. What factors did our team consider?

  1. Planetary Physics Normalization: We standardized physical differences across Earth, the Moon, and Mars for all 42 off-world zones (e.g., lunar vacuum having 0.00 aerosol optical depth vs. Martian dust opacity at 0.65, and 0.00 NDVI off-world), converting temperatures from Kelvin to Celsius and computing Delta T for fair mathematical comparison.
  2. Big-Data Hygiene & Map Performance: Scaling to 2,029 terrestrial sites required automated pandas pipelines to handle cloud-cover gaps and NaN pixel values in satellite imagery, alongside frontend marker optimization so rendering over two thousand locations remains fast and responsive.
  3. Open Science & Reproducibility: All 2,029 Earth profiles and 42 planetary targets are built on 100% free, open-source tools and public NASA datasets so any researcher can audit or expand the platform.
